passage: Tuesday night. I don't want to write this. In class today Arnab Sir called me to the board to solve 47 + 38 and I wrote 75. Everyone giggled. I stood there and my face went so hot. I said, "I'm stupid," quietly, and I didn't look up. Sir said, "Gopika, that was a wrong answer, not a wrong you." I didn't know what to say. At recess I sat behind the water tank. Later Sir asked if I wanted to redo it with him after school, just us. I nodded. We did it with sticks. Maybe I'll go tomorrow. I still feel small, but a bit less. — Gopika

qa.q: What sum did Arnab Sir ask Gopika to solve?
qa.a: He asked her to solve 47 + 38.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when she said "I'm stupid" and hid behind the water tank, and what might Sir's words have done?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and humiliated in front of the class. Sir's words separated the wrong answer from her as a person, which may have made it a little safer for her to try again.

qa.q: How could Arnab Sir keep supporting Gopika?
qa.a: He can keep offering private, low-pressure practice, praise her effort, and avoid calling her to the board when she feels unsafe, until her confidence returns.

qa.q: How might the classmates who giggled see the moment?
qa.a: Some may have giggled from surprise or habit without realising how much it hurt. Seeing Gopika hide could help them understand.

grounding: A child humiliated by failure calls herself stupid and hides, while an adult separates the person from the act and offers safety.

passage: At the village school in Bhojpur, Sonali dropped the school trophy while carrying it to the stage, and the little cup rolled under the bench. The hall laughed. Sonali stood frozen, then bolted out to the field and crouched behind the neem tree. Saurabh, the peon, found her there. "It's just a dent," he said, holding the cup. "Steel mends." She whispered, "Everyone saw me. I'm useless." Saurabh sat down on the grass at a distance. "You carried it the whole way from the office. One slip. That's not useless." After a while he handed her the cup and walked back beside her.

qa.q: Where did Sonali hide after dropping the trophy?
qa.a: She hid behind the neem tree on the field.

qa.q: What did Sonali mean by whispering "I'm useless", and how do her actions show it?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and humiliated, so she ran out and hid. She judged herself as a whole person instead of seeing one slip.

qa.q: What could an adult do when a child hides after a mistake?
qa.a: Stay calm and close, keep a little distance, name the mistake as small, and remind the child what they did right, as Saurabh did.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see Sonali's slip?
qa.a: Saurabh sees a dent in a cup that can be mended. He seems to view it as a simple accident rather than something to be ashamed of.

grounding: A child who fails publicly hides and says she is useless, and an adult separates the person from the act and offers safety.

passage:
At the swimming pool in Rotterdam, the class took turns for the floating test. Yara lay back, sank, and came up spluttering while the others watched from the edge. Someone laughed.
She climbed out, grabbed her towel and disappeared into the changing room. When the coach, Anders, knocked, she was sitting on the bench with the towel over her head.
"I'm so stupid," came her voice. "Everyone can float except me."
Anders sat on the other end of the bench, not too close. "You sank today. That's one try at one skill. It doesn't make you stupid."
The towel stayed on.
"Next week you can practise in the shallow end with me first, before anyone watches. Deal?"
After a long pause, the towel slipped down a little. "Only if nobody's looking," Yara said.

qa.q: Where did Anders find Yara after the test?
qa.a: In the changing room, sitting on the bench with the towel over her head.

qa.q: What does the towel over Yara's head suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt ashamed and humiliated, wanting to hide after sinking in front of the class; saying "I'm so stupid" shows she blamed herself, not just the try.

qa.q: Which part of Anders's response helped, and why?
qa.a: Separating the one failed try from who Yara is, and offering private practice first, helped because it gave her safety instead of more watching eyes.

qa.q: How might the classmate who laughed see the moment later?
qa.a: That classmate may not have meant much by it, but if they noticed Yara hiding, they might feel sorry for adding to her embarrassment.

grounding: A child humiliated by failing a swimming test hides and calls herself stupid, and the coach separates her from the act and offers safety.

passage:
In Class 6B, Afreen Ma'am asked Irawati to read the paragraph aloud. Irawati stumbled on "necessary," then on "environment." Someone at the back giggled.
She stopped reading. Her face went red. She put her head down on the desk and did not lift it for the rest of the period, even when her name was called for attendance.
At the bell, Afreen Ma'am waited until the room was empty. "Irawati, can I sit here?"
A small nod into her arms.
"Those were two hard words. Getting stuck on them doesn't change what I think of you."
Irawati muttered, "I'm the worst reader in the class."
"You're a reader who needs a little more practice with long words. That's different. Want to practise with me at lunch on Thursdays?"
Irawati lifted her head, just enough to nod.

qa.q: Which two words did Irawati stumble on?
qa.a: "Necessary" and "environment."

qa.q: Why did Irawati keep her head down even at attendance?
qa.a: She felt deeply ashamed and embarrassed after the giggle, so much that she wanted to hide rather than be seen by anyone.

qa.q: What did Afreen Ma'am do that fits a child who feels ashamed?
qa.a: She waited until the room was empty, told Irawati that stumbling didn't change how she saw her, and offered private practice, which gave safety.

qa.q: If you were the child who giggled, what might you not have noticed?
qa.a: You might not have noticed how one giggle made Irawati feel she was the worst reader, turning a small mistake into shame.

grounding: A child humiliated while reading aloud goes silent and calls herself the worst, and a teacher separates the person from the mistake.

passage:
My sister Binita came home from school and went straight to her room without saying hello to anyone. She didn't come out for dinner. Through the door I heard her say, "I'm useless, I'm just useless."
I didn't know what happened. Maybe it was the maths test. Maybe someone said something.
Papa knocked and went in. I stayed in the corridor. I heard him say quietly, "One bad test is about one test, not about you. You're still my Binita."
She cried. He stayed in there a long time.
Later she came out with red eyes and ate cold rice. Papa sat with her. The next morning she let Papa help her correct the paper.
- Zubin

qa.q: What did Binita say through the door?
qa.a: "I'm useless, I'm just useless."

qa.q: What might Binita have been feeling when she skipped dinner?
qa.a: She was probably ashamed and upset about something at school, maybe the maths test, though Zubin can't be sure what happened.

qa.q: What did Papa do that helped?
qa.a: He went to her, separated the test from who she is, and stayed with her, which gave her enough safety to come out and later correct the paper.

qa.q: How did Zubin experience that evening?
qa.a: Zubin was worried and unsure, standing in the corridor without knowing what had happened or how to help.

grounding: A sibling observes a child hiding after a failure and calling herself useless, and a parent separating the person from the result.

passage:
Tuesday: Pranav dropped the easy catch that lost the inter-class match. While the others cheered the winners, he hid behind the equipment shed with his face on his knees. "I'm so stupid. I'm useless," he muttered when Chandrika Ma'am found him. She sat on an upturned bucket nearby. "You dropped one catch. That's something that happened, not who you are. You're safe here. Take your time."
Thursday: Pranav came to practice but stood at the very back. Ma'am threw him easy catches, one after another, and said only, "Watch the ball into your hands."
The following Monday: A high ball came his way in the lunchtime game. Pranav caught it, looked round for Ma'am, and grinned.

qa.q: Where did Pranav hide after the match?
qa.a: Behind the equipment shed.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when he muttered that he was stupid?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and humiliated, turning one dropped catch into a judgement about his whole self.

qa.q: What helped Pranav return to the game?
qa.a: Ma'am's words separating the catch from who he is, then quiet practice with easy catches and one simple tip, without raking up the loss.

qa.q: How might Chandrika Ma'am have seen Pranav behind the shed?
qa.a: She likely saw a child who needed safety more than a lesson, so she sat nearby instead of lecturing.

grounding: It illustrates a child hiding and calling himself stupid after a failure, and an adult separating the act from the person and offering safety.
